newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Kohl, in Clinton footsteps, to visit Australia.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, in Clinton footsteps, to visit Australia.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl arrives in Australia's tropical north on Friday for a weekend of relaxation at the Great Barrier Reef before a day of political talks and a tourist trip around Sydney harbour.
Kohl, 67 and the West's longest-serving leader, will be following in the footsteps of U.S. President Bill Clinton when he arrives at this Queensland beach resort on Friday evening.
Clinton and his wife Hillary visited the same palm-lined paradise last November, soon after the U.S. president won his second term in office.
With domestic political problems far away, the German leader will be spoilt for choice for weekend activities -- paddling on the Reef, game-fishing or visiting the Queensland rain forest.
On Sunday evening, with a delegation of senior business people, Kohl will fly south to the Australian capital Canberra for a day of talks with Australian political leaders.
After Clinton and a visit this week by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Kohl will be the third major power leader to visit Canberra in little over five months
With no burning bilateral issues to discuss, the talks will be an opportunity to review and strengthen trade and diplomatic ties between the two nations.

"The Chancellor's visit is a valuable opportunity to reaffirm the importance of the relationship between our countries and our shared commitment to expanding our ties," Australian Prime Minister John Howard said this week.
"I also look forward to discussing with the Chancellor the scope for cooperation between Australia and Germany in pursuing our economic interests in the Asia-Pacific and in Europe."
One international issue likely to be on the agenda -- as it was with both Clinton and Hashimoto -- will be the need for binding international controls on greenhouse gas emissions.

Howard's government, elected 13 months ago, has shifted from the policy of the previous Labor administration on the need for compulsory targets to cut emissions of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, arguing that such targets would damage Australian industry.

Germany is at the forefront of a European plan to toughen the scheme at the third international Climate Change conference in Kyoto, Japan in December and the United States has also been putting pressure on Canberra to fall into line on the issue with its Western allies.

Kohl's visit to Australia is his second since he became Chancellor in 1982 but his first since German reunification. His first visit in 1988 was cut short by the death of a prominent German politician.
Kohl will round off his visit on Tuesday in Sydney, where he is expected to take a trip around the city's reknowned harbour before flying off for an official visit to New Zealand.
